To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
3 occasions warming and handling alone, 3 occasions warming, handling and taking 32μl blood samples, or 3 occasions taking 32μ l blood samples, had no permanent adverse effect on maternal health.
the effect of microsamples on mouse fetuses in the EFD study design is minimal and the number of satellite animals can be reduced by using 3 microsamples per mouse.
taking 3 microsamples on gestation day (GD)16 of 32μl of blood from pregnant CD1 mice did not have any permanent adverse effects on the pregnant dams or their fetuses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing an EFD design that minimizes the use of satellite animals.
the use of microsampling in EFD studies and the effects of microsampling on fetal weights and pregnant mice.
the development of an alternative method for taking blood samples in the embryofetald development study design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
taking up to 3 microsamples (32 μL) of whole blood at the end of mouse organogenesis (gestation days 15-18) had no permanent adverse effect on maternal health or on the development of fetuses.
3 samples of 32μl taken from pregnant mice on gestation day16 has no adverse effects on fetal development or maternal health.
3 samples of 32μl taken on gestation day (GD) 16 had no adverse effects on fetal weight or maternal health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
3 microsamples on gestation day (GD) 16 had no permanent adverse maternal or fetal effects and that 6 samples could be taken on GD 16 without adverse effects on maternal body weight gain.
6 occasion warming, handling and taking of 3 x 32μL microsamples on gestation day16 in mice is acceptable for EFD study designs, and can reduce satellite animal usage.
the effects of taking multiple microsamples on gestation day16 were minimal, and that 3 samples per timepoint was the optimal number to obtain composite toxicokinetic data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of taking microsamples on pregnant mice and fetal weights are transient and do not have toxicologically significant effects.
the effects of microsampling are not permanent and can be minimized by limiting the number of occasions that animals are warmed and handled.
microsampling is a viable alternative to the current practice of taking 0.2 mL blood samples from pregnant animals in EFD studies.
